## HueMux v0.0.2-alpha.18 — Recording resolution no longer slows the lights

> **Alpha.** Performance work, from the sluggishness you reported and the 4.1
> inbound fps in your log.

### What was wrong

One buffer was serving two things that want opposite sizes. The colour engine
reduces every frame to a 64×36 grid and does not care how big it started; a
recording cares a great deal. Both were fed from a single full-resolution copy,
so the expensive work happened whether or not anything needed it.

At 942×1920 that meant, per frame: a per-pixel copy of 1.8 million pixels doing
three separate memory reads each, 5.4MB pushed across into the Go engine, then
copied again, and finally converted to video — all so it could be averaged down
to 2304 cells.

So raising the resolution for a video slowed your lights. That is backwards.

### What changed

The frame is now read once for each consumer, and each gets what it needs:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Frame given to the colour engine | 942×1920 | 235×480 |
| Data per frame | 5.4 MB | 338 KB |
| Frame rate | up to 60/s | 30/s |

Reads are done a row at a time instead of a pixel at a time, which is a memory
copy rather than millions of individual accesses. The recorder now reads the
capture surface directly, with no intermediate copy at all.

You suggested a downscale checkbox. I made it unconditional instead, because
there is nothing to trade: 480 pixels on the long edge still gives the engine
about seven samples per grid cell in each direction, so it cannot tell the
difference. It averages blocks rather than picking one pixel — cheaper sampling
looks identical on flat colour but aliases on text, and that reaches the eye as
colours shimmering while the screen is still.

### The slider is now "Recording resolution"

Because that is all it does now. Light sync always works from a downscaled
copy, so this only affects how sharp a recording is and what the mirror costs
in battery. Leave it low unless you are recording.

### Verifying this

I cannot compile Kotlin here, so I modelled the index arithmetic against
realistic memory layouts — padded and packed strides, odd dimensions, sizes
from 64×64 to 942×1920 — and checked every read stays in bounds and every
output is written exactly once. That found two bugs before you could: a stale
row averaged into the bottom edge of every frame, and a buffer left undeclared
when the old one was removed.

Still unmeasured on hardware. If sync still feels slow at a low recording
resolution, the next suspect is the bridge — your log shows its event stream
dropping and timing out repeatedly, which I have not touched.
